## Date, Place, and Recipients

Joseph Smith dictated this revelation at **Kirtland, Ohio, on March 7, 1831**. It is addressed broadly to "ye people of my church" (vv. 1, 6) rather than to a single person. The Church was not yet a year old (organized April 6, 1830).

## The Situation in Early 1831

- **The move to Ohio:** In December 1830 and January 1831, revelations directed the New York Saints to gather to Ohio (D&C 37; 38:31–32). Joseph Smith arrived in Kirtland around **February 1, 1831**, and New York members followed through the spring. Kirtland already had a large group of converts from the mission of Oliver Cowdery, Parley P. Pratt, and others, who had passed through on their way to preach to Native Americans on the Missouri frontier.
- **Hostile reports:** Joseph Smith's history introduces this revelation by noting that many false reports and stories about the Church were being published and circulated to discourage people from investigating it. The revelation came, the history says, to the joy of the Saints. Its broad view of God's plan for the last days answered a time of ridicule and uncertainty.
- **The law and Zion:** A month earlier, D&C 42 ("the law") had promised that the location of the **New Jerusalem** would be revealed (D&C 42:9, 62). Members were eager to know when and where Zion would be built.
- **A millennial age:** Many American Christians in the early 1830s expected the Second Coming soon and read current events as signs of the end. D&C 45 addresses those expectations in Restoration terms.

## Connection to Joseph Smith's Bible Translation

This revelation is closely tied to Joseph Smith's **inspired revision of the Bible** (the Joseph Smith Translation, or JST).

- **Enoch (vv. 11–14):** Joseph had recently received the extended account of **Enoch and his city, Zion**, now Moses 7 (December 1830), which explains this revelation's reference to Enoch's city "reserved until a day of righteousness."
- **The New Testament (vv. 60–61):** The Lord tells Joseph that he may now begin translating the **New Testament**, where these things "shall be made known." Joseph began the New Testament the very next day, **March 8, 1831**, pausing his work on Genesis.
- **Matthew 24:** The Olivet Discourse retold in vv. 16–59 parallels Joseph's later revision of Matthew 24, published in the Pearl of Great Price as **Joseph Smith—Matthew**. Reading the two together is one of the best ways to study this section.

## The Olivet Discourse Background

In vv. 16–59 the Lord recounts what he taught his disciples on the Mount of Olives shortly before his crucifixion (Matthew 24; Mark 13; Luke 21). That discourse addressed two questions: when the temple would be destroyed (fulfilled when Rome destroyed Jerusalem in **AD 70**) and what signs would precede his Second Coming. D&C 45 keeps the two questions distinct and adds Restoration details: the **"times of the Gentiles"** (Luke 21:24) climax in a light that breaks forth as "the fulness of my gospel" (v. 28). It also includes material from Zechariah's prophecies of the Mount of Olives splitting (Zech. 14:4) and of the Jews recognizing the wounded Messiah (Zech. 12:10; 13:6).

## Zion and the Westward Gathering (vv. 64–71)

The command to "gather ye out from the eastern lands" and go "into the western countries" fit the Church's movement from New York to Ohio and anticipated the next step. The promised **New Jerusalem**, a city of refuge called Zion, echoes the Book of Mormon (Ether 13:2–10; 3 Nephi 20:22; 21:23–24) and Moses 7:62. Four months later, in **July 1831**, a revelation identified **Independence, Jackson County, Missouri**, as the center place of Zion (D&C 57).

## Reading the Prophecies in Their Time

- **"Wars in your own lands" (v. 63):** Early readers connected this warning with later revelation about civil conflict, especially D&C 87 (December 25, 1832), which foretold war beginning with the rebellion of South Carolina.
- **"A desolating sickness" (v. 31):** Some early Saints associated this with the **cholera** pandemic that reached North America in 1832. The text itself places it among the signs of the last days generally.
- **"Keep these things from going abroad" (v. 72):** The revelation was first meant for Church members. It was later published in the 1833 Book of Commandments and in later editions of the Doctrine and Covenants.

## Why It Matters

D&C 45 is the Restoration's most sustained treatment of the **signs of the Second Coming** before D&C 88 and Joseph Smith—Matthew. It links the ancient promises (Enoch's Zion, the restoration of Israel, the Olivet prophecies) to the young Church's own tasks: translating scripture, gathering, and building Zion. It also opens with one of the most personal portraits of Christ as **advocate** in scripture (vv. 3–5).

breakdown.title: Hearken to the Creator and Advocate
breakdown.summary: The Lord calls his church to hearken to the Creator of heaven and earth before the harvest is past. He presents Christ as the advocate pleading with the Father on the strength of his own sinless suffering, asking that believers be spared.

breakdown.title: The Light and the Everlasting Covenant
breakdown.summary: Christ declares himself Alpha and Omega and the light shining in darkness, who gives power to those who receive him to become sons of God. He has sent his everlasting covenant as a light, a standard, and a messenger to prepare his way, and invites all to come and reason with him.

breakdown.title: Enoch and His City
breakdown.summary: The Lord recalls Enoch and his people, taken from the earth and reserved as a city until a day of righteousness. Holy men sought that day as strangers and pilgrims and were promised to see it in the flesh.

breakdown.title: To the Disciples: Jerusalem's Destruction
breakdown.summary: The Lord recounts what he told his disciples about the signs of his coming. He first prophesied that the Jerusalem temple would be thrown down and that the Jews of that generation would be destroyed and scattered among all nations.

breakdown.title: Scattering and the Times of the Gentiles
breakdown.summary: The scattered remnant will be gathered again after the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled, when the fulness of the gospel breaks forth as a light many reject. Wars, commotion, cold love, an overflowing scourge, desolating sickness, and earthquakes mark that generation, while disciples stand in holy places.

breakdown.title: The Parable of the Fig Tree
breakdown.summary: When the troubled disciples hear these things, the Lord comforts them with the parable of the fig tree: as tender leaves show summer is near, the signs will show that his coming is near.

breakdown.title: Signs in Heaven and the Coming in Glory
breakdown.summary: Those who fear the Lord will watch for signs in the heavens and the earth: blood, fire, smoke, a darkened sun, and a moon turned to blood. The Lord comes in the clouds with power and glory, the righteous dead rise to meet him, and his arm falls upon the nations.

breakdown.title: The Mount of Olives and the Jews' Recognition
breakdown.summary: The Lord sets his foot on the Mount of Olives, which splits in two, and the earth and heavens shake. The Jews ask about the wounds in his hands and feet, recognize Jesus as the crucified Son of God, and weep for their rejection of their king.

breakdown.title: The Millennium and the Ten Virgins
breakdown.summary: The heathen nations are redeemed and Satan is bound. The parable of the ten virgins is fulfilled: the wise, who received truth and took the Holy Spirit as their guide, abide the day and inherit the earth with the Lord as their king and lawgiver.

breakdown.title: Translate the New Testament
breakdown.summary: Joseph Smith is told he will learn more of this chapter only through translating the New Testament, which he is now authorized to begin, because great things await the Saints.

breakdown.title: Gathering West and the New Jerusalem
breakdown.summary: Warning of wars soon to come in their own lands, the Lord commands the elders to gather west, preach repentance, and pool their means to purchase an inheritance. There they will build the New Jerusalem, Zion, a city of peace and refuge that the wicked will fear and the righteous will reach with songs of everlasting joy.

breakdown.title: Keep These Things Until It Is Expedient
breakdown.summary: The Saints are to keep this revelation from the world until their work is done. When the Lord appears, he will be terrible to the wicked and all nations will fear his power.

45.literaryUnit:
## Genre

D&C 45 is a **revelation in the voice of the Lord**: direct, first-person divine speech addressed to the Church. Within that frame it combines four forms:

- **Prophetic exhortation:** repeated calls to "hearken"
- **Intercessory speech:** Christ's plea to the Father (vv. 3–5)
- **Apocalyptic prophecy:** signs of the last days (vv. 16–59)
- **Practical commandment:** translation, gathering, and secrecy (vv. 60–75)

## A Speech Within a Speech

The section's most distinctive feature is its **frame structure**:

1. **Present-day address (vv. 1–15):** Christ speaks to the Church of 1831.
2. **Embedded retrospective discourse (vv. 16–59):** Christ quotes what he said to his ancient disciples on the Mount of Olives ("I will show it plainly as I showed it unto my disciples," v. 16). Even the disciples' reaction is reported (v. 34).
3. **Present-day application (vv. 60–75):** The voice returns to 1831 with direct instructions.

The frame lets the revelation present the ancient prophecy as newly restored and plain. It ties the disciples' anxious questions in Jerusalem to the Saints' questions in Kirtland.

## The "Hearken" Refrain

The opening is structured by repeated summons: "Hearken" (v. 1), "hearken unto my voice" (v. 2), "Listen to him" (v. 3), "Hearken… listen together" (v. 6), "hearken ye together" (v. 11), and "hearken and I will reason with you" (v. 15). Each summons introduces a new portrait of Christ: **Creator** (v. 1), **Advocate** (vv. 3–5), **Light and Covenant-giver** (vv. 7–10), and **God of Enoch** (vv. 11–14). The phrase "reason… as with men in days of old" (vv. 10, 15) bridges the introduction into the prophecy.

## Christ's Plea (vv. 3–5)

This short passage is a **prayer embedded in a revelation**. Christ addresses the Father in direct speech with a three-part appeal: *behold* the sufferings, *behold* the blood, *spare* these my brethren. Its legal imagery of an advocate "pleading your cause" frames the whole section: the coming judgment is announced by the one who intercedes for those facing it.

## Intertextual Weaving

D&C 45 is densely built from biblical language, recombined and expanded:

- **John's prologue** (vv. 7–8): Alpha and Omega, the light shining in darkness, coming to his own, power to become sons of God (John 1:5, 11–12).
- **Jeremiah 8:20** (v. 2): the summer past and the harvest ended.
- **Psalm 95 / Hebrews 3** (v. 6): "while it is called today… harden not your hearts."
- **Hebrews 11:13–16** (vv. 12–14): strangers and pilgrims seeking a city.
- **Matthew 24 / Luke 21** (vv. 16–44): temple destruction, wars and rumors of wars, love waxing cold, the fig tree, the times of the Gentiles.
- **Joel 2:30–31** (vv. 41–42): blood, fire, vapors of smoke; the sun darkened and the moon turned to blood.
- **1 Thessalonians 4:16–17** (v. 45): the trump sounds and the saints rise to meet the Lord.
- **Zechariah 14:4; 12:10; 13:6** (vv. 48–53): the Mount of Olives splitting; the Jews looking on the pierced one; wounds received "in the house of my friends."
- **Matthew 25:1–13** (vv. 56–57): the ten virgins, reinterpreted as those who take the Holy Spirit for their guide.

## Motifs That Bind the Section

- **Light:** Christ is the light that darkness does not comprehend (v. 7). The covenant is sent as a light (v. 9), and in the last days "a light shall break forth" (vv. 28, 36). Those who reject it "perceive not the light" (v. 29).
- **Summer and harvest:** "the summer shall be past" (v. 2) is answered by the fig tree's leaves showing "summer is now nigh" (v. 37). The same seasonal image moves from warning to hope.
- **City:** Enoch's city reserved in heaven (v. 12) and the New Jerusalem on earth (vv. 66–71) bracket the prophecy. The city sought by "holy men" of old becomes the Saints' own task.
- **Fear:** "Be not troubled" (v. 35) for the disciples, versus the "terror of the Lord" for the wicked (vv. 67, 74–75). Zion is "terrible" to its enemies (v. 70) but a place of safety for the Saints (v. 66).

## Climactic Recognition Scene (vv. 51–53)

The prophecy reaches its emotional peak in a short **dialogue**. The Jews ask about the wounds, and Christ answers with three escalating "I am" declarations: he who was *lifted up*, *Jesus that was crucified*, and *the Son of God* (v. 52). Their weeping follows, and the scene turns from cosmic catastrophe to personal reconciliation.

## Closing

The section ends where it began, with the Lord's power over all nations, and closes with the formal **"Even so. Amen."** It moves from creation (v. 1) to consummation (v. 75), and from the Lord as advocate to the Lord as judge.
